paragraphs: **Rabbi Yossi, when named without qualification—son of Chalafta.**

It is generally agreed that an unqualified “Rabbi Yossi” means the son of Rabbi Chalafta, who was the leading sage in Sepphoris. This is also Rashi’s view at the end of [Zevachim 58b](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Zevachim.58b).[^1]

His family and ancestry are explicitly described in [Jerusalem Talmud, Ta’anit 4:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Taanit.4.2): “A genealogical scroll was found in Jerusalem, and in it was written: ‘Rabbi Yossi ben Chalafta was descended from Yonadav ben Rekhav.’” It is known that Yonadav ben Rekhav’s family descended from Jethro. [Sanhedrin 104a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.104a) records Rabbi Yochanan’s statement that, as a reward for “Call him, that he may eat bread,” Jethro’s descendants merited to sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, as it says: “The families of the scribes … these are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rekhav.”

Yonadav ben Rekhav’s family always lived in the Land of Israel. [II Kings 10:15](https://www.sefaria.org/II_Kings.10.15) says that Jehu went from there and encountered Yehonadav ben Rekhav. [Jeremiah 35](https://www.sefaria.org/Jeremiah.35) relates that Yonadav ben Rekhav commanded his children not to drink wine, build houses, or plant vineyards. Because they kept their father’s command, Jeremiah told them in God’s name: “Yonadav ben Rekhav shall never lack a man standing before Me.” Jeremiah’s prophecy was fulfilled even in later times, when these sages sprang from his line: our masters Rabbi Chalafta, his son Rabbi Yossi, and Rabbi Yossi’s five sons.

[Yoma 66b](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.66b) quotes the Mishnah: “They made a ramp for him because of the Babylonians.” Rabba bar bar Chana said that they were not Babylonians. A baraita likewise teaches Rabbi Yehuda’s statement: “They were not Babylonians but Alexandrians”—and, because people disliked the Babylonians, they called them by that name. Rabbi Yossi said to him: “May your mind be at ease, for you have put my mind at ease.” Rashi explains that Rabbi Yossi’s family came from Babylonia, and the accusation therefore troubled him. [Menachot 100a](https://www.sefaria.org/Menachot.100a), however, quotes the Mishnah’s statement that “the Babylonians ate it raw,” and then says that Rabba bar bar Chana reported in Rabbi Yochanan’s name that they were not Babylonians. Its baraita attributes this explanation to Rabbi Yossi, and Rabbi Yehuda tells him: “May your mind be at ease.” There Rashi explains that Rabbi Yehuda’s family came from Babylonia, so he was pleased by Rabbi Yossi’s words. *Dikdukei Soferim* gives the reading in Yoma as in Menachot: Rabbi Yehuda said this to Rabbi Yossi. Indeed, [Menachot 45a](https://www.sefaria.org/Menachot.45a) also has Rabbi Yehuda tell Rabbi Yossi: “May your mind be at ease, for you have put my mind at ease.”[^2]

The valuable *Darkhei ha-Mishnah*, page 164, and *Mevo ha-Mishnah*, page 178, say that Rabbi Yehuda’s family did not come from Babylonia. They read all these passages as Rabbi Yossi saying to Rabbi Yehuda, “May your mind be at ease,” and explain that the error arose from the abbreviation ר״י. But the great author of the work abbreviated דה״ד, part I, page 120, has already demonstrated that neither Rabbi Yehuda’s nor Rabbi Yossi’s family came from Babylonia: both came only from the Land of Israel. Rather, the meaning of Yoma and Menachot is this: the Mishnah spoke disparagingly of the Babylonians, whereas our holy masters knew well that the Jews living in Babylonia were the choicest of the nation, with no disqualified lineage mingled among them. Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Yossi was therefore deeply troubled: how could the Babylonians have behaved so? When he heard from his colleague that they were not actually Babylonians, but people from Babylonia who had settled long before in Alexandria and whom the Alexandrians continued to call “Babylonians,” he said, “May your mind be at ease.” His colleague had removed a reproach from the Babylonians, the nation’s prized community. Let us return to our subject.[^3]

His father, Rabbi Chalafta, lived long enough to see Rabban Gamliel the Elder, as [Shabbat 115a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.115a) records. He was the leading sage in Sepphoris, as [Ta’anit 16b](https://www.sefaria.org/Taanit.16b) records, and transmitted much of his learning to his son Rabbi Yossi. “A gourd is recognizable from its stalk”: he was made for greatness. [Midrash Tehillim, chapter 83](https://www.sefaria.org/Midrash_Tehillim.83), relates that, when Rabbi Yossi ben Chalafta was a boy playing with other boys, a man saw him and said, “Your father ought to be told.” He answered: “By your life, what concern is it of yours? If you tell my father, he will strike me, and you will be training your tongue to speak slander.” We also find him stating a ruling in his father’s name: [Kelim 26:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kelim.26.6), “Rabbi Yossi declares it pure on his father’s authority”; and [Bekhorot 26a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.26a), “Rabbi Yossi said: Father Chalafta admits that this is permitted.” [^21] His father was so sacred in his eyes that he said in [Sanhedrin 80a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.80a), “Even if Father Chalafta were among them.” He also related many incidents concerning his father, as explained in his father’s entry.

His principal teacher, however, was Rabbi Akiva. [Pesachim 18a](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.18a) explicitly says that Rabbi Yossi stated his ruling according to the position of his teacher Rabbi Akiva. He reports actual rulings by Rabbi Akiva in [Kilayim 7:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kilayim.7.5) and [Terumot 4:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Terumot.4.3). At the end of [Tosefta Parah, chapter 4](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Parah.4), he says: “On this ruling I spoke up before Rabbi Akiva.” [Yevamot 62b](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.62b) relates that, when all Rabbi Akiva’s pupils died, the world was desolate until he went to our masters in the south and taught them—Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yossi, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua. They restored Torah at that time. Rabbi Yossi nevertheless received ordination from Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, not Rabbi Akiva. [Sanhedrin 14a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.14a) explicitly records that Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava ordained him between Usha and Shefar’am during the persecution.

He received teachings not only from Rabbi Akiva, but also from the other great sages of Yavneh. In [Shabbat 125a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.125a), he gives testimony on Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov’s authority. [Eruvin 36a](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin.36a) says that Avtolmos was his teacher. He also speaks in Rabban Gamliel’s name in [Tosefta Kiddushin, chapter 1](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Kiddushin.1); in Rabbi Yehoshua’s name in [Pesachim 103a](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.103a); and in Rabbi Yishmael’s name in [Bava Kamma 54b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Kamma.54b) and [Zevachim 60b](https://www.sefaria.org/Zevachim.60b). He likewise sat at Rabbi Tarfon’s feet. [Tosefta Shevi’it, chapter 4](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Sheviit.4), records Rabbi Yehuda’s account, “There was an incident … and we ate … on Rabbi Tarfon’s authority,” to which Rabbi Yossi replies, “Is that evidence? I was there with you.” [Tosefta Kelim, Bava Batra, chapter 5](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Kelim_Batra.5), has Rabbi Yossi report that Yonatan ben Charsha of Gennesar posed a question before the elders in Yavneh.

He also received many teachings from Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and related practical rulings in his name. At the end of [Ketubot, chapter 1](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Ketubot.1), Rabbi Yossi tells of an incident involving a young woman, in which Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri ruled, “If the majority …” In [Tosefta Shevi’it, chapter 4](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Sheviit.4), he relates an incident in which they went to consult Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri. [Tosefta Megillah, chapter 2](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Megillah.2), has him report that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri read the Megillah in Sepphoris at night. He speaks in his name in [Tosefta Kelim, Bava Kamma, chapters 2 and 4](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Kelim_Kamma), [Bava Batra, chapter 7](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Kelim_Batra.7), and *Torat Kohanim*, Shemini, chapter 7. In [Bekhorot 10b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.10b), he also says: “Nimos, the brother of Rabbi Yehoshua ha-Garsi, told me.”

He witnessed his people’s affliction: all his teachers and the sages of Israel were led to slaughter. He saw his birthplace in danger, as [Tosefta Megillah, chapter 2](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Megillah.2), records. [Numbers Rabbah, at the beginning of chapter 23](https://www.sefaria.org/Bamidbar_Rabbah.23), likewise says that, in Rabbi Elazar ben Perata’s time, harsh orders from the government reached the leading men of Sepphoris, and they fled. Apparently Sepphoris was then laid waste. This explains [Bava Batra 75b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.75b): “Rabbi Yossi says: I saw Sepphoris in its prosperity, and it had 130,000 marketplaces.” Possibly he then fled to Asia, as [Bava Metzia 84b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Metzia.84b) indicates.[^4]

From there he came and settled temporarily in the south with his colleagues, and Rabbi Akiva transmitted his Torah to them. Later he saw his holy teacher imprisoned. At the end of [Gittin, chapter 6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Gittin.6), Rabbi Yossi says, “We told the messenger”—Rabbi Chanina of Ono, who brought a ruling from Rabbi Akiva in prison. When Rabbi Akiva was killed, Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava remained like a firebrand rescued from the flames; he risked his life to ordain them. They then scattered in every direction, and all the academies in the Land of Israel ceased to function. They could not even intercalate years or establish months there. Chananya, Rabbi Yehoshua’s nephew, consequently intercalated years in Babylonia, at Nehar Pekod, since he had left no one his equal in the Land of Israel.

Eventually God had mercy on the surviving remnant. Emperor Hadrian died amid dreadful illness, bitterness of spirit, and bitterness of soul; the harsh decrees eased somewhat. The sages of Israel, Rabbi Akiva’s pupils, then rallied and gathered in the valley of Rimmon. [Jerusalem Talmud, Chagigah 3:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Chagigah.3.1), relates that seven elders assembled there: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yossi, Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Nechemya, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, and Rabbi Yochanan the Sandal-maker. They said: “Anyone able to intercalate the year who does not do so is as though he worshipped idols.” They then sent to Chananya, Rabbi Yehoshua’s nephew, in Nehar Pekod, telling him to stop intercalating years outside the Land of Israel, as [Berakhot 63a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.63a) explains.[^5]

When the decrees eased a little further, they gathered at Usha. [Song of Songs Rabbah 2:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Shir_HaShirim_Rabbah.2.5) says: “At the close of the persecution, our masters entered Usha”—Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Nechemya, Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yossi, Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, Rabbi Eliezer the son of Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. They sent word to the elders of Galilee: “Whoever has learned should come and teach.” They honored Rabbi Yehuda as the principal speaker because he was a native of the town. [^23] They did not remain long, however, but left for Yavneh for a short time. Even there they were not allowed to intercalate years and had to send Rabbi Meir to Asia to do so, as [Megillah 18b](https://www.sefaria.org/Megillah.18b) records. This explains [Shabbat 33b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.33b): “When our masters entered the vineyard at Yavneh, Rabbi Yehuda was there …”

There occurred the incident in which Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yossi, and Rabbi Shimon sat together, with Yehuda ben Gerim beside them. Rabbi Yehuda praised Rome’s achievements; Rabbi Yossi remained silent; Rabbi Shimon spoke against them. Yehuda ben Gerim went and recounted their words, and the government heard of them. It decreed: “Yehuda, who exalted us, shall be exalted; Shimon, who disparaged us, shall be killed.” Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai then fled to the cave with his son. Rabbi Yossi, who had remained silent, was sentenced to exile in Sepphoris.

The work abbreviated דה״ד wishes to emend this to “exile **from** Sepphoris,” and later scholars share that view. But they have misread the matter. Rabbi Yossi’s punishment was to be confined to his birthplace: he was not to go beyond the city’s walls, so that he could not associate with his colleagues.

Although Rabbi Yehuda found favor with the government and undoubtedly tried to mitigate Rabbi Yossi’s sentence—as [Berakhot 63b](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.63b) records, when our masters entered the vineyard at Yavneh, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi were there; Rabbi Yehuda, principal speaker everywhere, opened the discussion, and Rabbi Yossi spoke in honor of their hosts—Rabbi Shimon is not mentioned with them because he had already fled. Apparently the appeal did not succeed: Rabbi Yossi had to go to Sepphoris. Thus [Shabbat 38a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.38a) records Rabbi Chanina’s statement that, when Rabbi Yossi went to Sepphoris, he found hot water that had remained on a stove and did not forbid it, but forbade eggs that had shriveled through cooking.

As we said above, Sepphoris had been devastated. When people returned and settled there again, Rabbi Yossi, as the city’s leading sage, had to establish regulations, since it was virtually a new city. This explains his statement in [Kiddushin 2:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kiddushin.2.5): “Even someone who had been a witness in the old court of Sepphoris.” [Sanhedrin 19b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.19b) records his ordinance that a woman should not walk in the marketplace with her son following behind her, because of an incident that had occurred. The city had been resettled and still had few Jewish inhabitants. Thieves came to abduct a woman’s child. When she began to cry out, one of the assailants told her, “Come, and I will show you your son”; when she went there, they violated her. He also ordained that women should converse in the privy.[^6]

This explains [Eruvin 86b](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin.86b): “The incident that occurred in Sepphoris—on whose authority did it occur? Was it not on Rabbi Yossi’s?” [Sanhedrin 109a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.109a) likewise relates that Rabbi Yossi lectured in Sepphoris, and that night 300 burglaries were committed there. People came to complain: “You showed the thieves a way!” He answered: “Could I have known that thieves would come?” He established a great academy there. [Sanhedrin 32b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.32b) tells people to follow Rabbi Yossi to Sepphoris. Thus, when the sages settled in Usha and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was appointed nasi, they appointed Rabbi Meir as the sage, Rabbi Natan as av bet din, and Rabbi Yehuda as the teacher of the nasi’s household. Rabbi Yossi could take no part with them, because he was forbidden to leave Sepphoris.

His stature was so great that Elijah was said to visit him regularly. [Sanhedrin 113b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.113b) relates that Rabbi Yossi preached in Sepphoris that Father Elijah was irascible. Elijah, who used to visit him, then concealed himself for three days. When he returned, Rabbi Yossi asked, “Why did the Master not come?” He answered: “You called me irascible!” Rabbi Yossi replied: “Here we have it before us: the Master is taking offense.” In [Yevamot 63a](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.63a), Rabbi Yossi meets Elijah and asks about “I will make him a helpmate.” In [Berakhot 3a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.3a), Rabbi Yossi relates: “Once I entered one of Jerusalem’s ruins … Elijah, of blessed memory, came and stood guard at the entrance for me”; Elijah called him “my son.”[^7]

Later, when the decrees were annulled, we also find Rabbi Yossi in Usha. [Horayot 13b](https://www.sefaria.org/Horayot.13b) relates that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Natan wished to remove Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel from the office of nasi. When he learned of their plan, he expelled them from the academy. They sat outside, wrote slips containing difficult questions, and sent them inside. Rabbi Yossi then said: “Torah is outside, and we are inside?” At his intervention Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allowed them to return to their places.

He was greatly beloved by the nasi, who recognized his stature and received rulings from him. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel speaks in Rabbi Yossi’s name in [Megillah 6b](https://www.sefaria.org/Megillah.6b), [Moed Katan 12b](https://www.sefaria.org/Moed_Katan.12b), [Avodah Zarah 75a](https://www.sefaria.org/Avodah_Zarah.75a), and [Niddah 25b](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.25b). In [Berakhot 26a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.26a), Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: “Once my eyes troubled me in Caesarea, and Rabbi Yossi Beribbi permitted me …” Rashi explains *Beribbi* as the outstanding, incisive sage of his generation. [Pesachim 100a](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.100a) relates that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yossi were dining in Acre when the Sabbath began. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel asked Rabbi Yossi Beribbi, “Would you like us to interrupt and take account of our colleague Rabbi Yehuda’s view?” He replied: “Every day you favor my view over Rabbi Yehuda’s, and now you favor Rabbi Yehuda’s over mine? ‘Will you even overpower the queen with me in the house?’”
**His rulings in the Mishnah.**

Rabbi Yossi is mentioned in every tractate of the Mishnah except Bikkurim, Chagigah, Horayot, Me’ilah, and Tamid. In the following tractates he appears only once: [Berakhot 2:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Berakhot.2.3); [Challah 4:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Challah.4.8); Bikkurim—although he is absent from its first three chapters, he appears in [4:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bikkurim.4.5); [Beitzah 4:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Beitzah.4.2); [Megillah 2:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Megillah.2.3); [Bava Kamma 4:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Kamma.4.4); [Shevuot 7:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Shevuot.7.4); [Avot 4:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Pirkei_Avot.4.6); and [Kinnim 1:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kinnim.1.4). The Rabbi Yossi who appears in Avot 2:4 is Rabbi Yossi ha-Kohen, a pupil of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai; *Seder ha-Dorot* erred in this.[^8]

In each of Eduyot, Middot, and Negaim he is mentioned twice, and in Kelim thirty-four times. In all, he appears fifty-four times in Zera’im, fifty-four in Moed, thirty-three in Nashim, twenty-nine in Nezikin, thirty-nine in Kodashim, and 131 in Toharot: 340 rulings in the Mishnah. *Seder ha-Dorot* counts Shabbat 6:6, where our reading is Rabbi Meir, and omits [Makkot 2:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Makkot.2.3) and [Mikvaot 6:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Mikvaot.6.5).

Most of his disagreements are with the anonymous Mishnah—approximately 161 times. He disagrees with “the sages” six times; with his colleague Rabbi Yehuda about fifty times; with Rabbi Meir about forty-two times; and with Rabbi Shimon about fifteen times. In the disputes with Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yossi is always listed last except in [Ma’aser Sheni 4:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Maaser_Sheni.4.6) and [Berakhot 2:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Berakhot.2.3), where Rabbi Yossi comes first.

He also disagreed with Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua in [Eruvin 6:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Eruvin.6.5)—the text there says “in Rabbi Eliezer’s time,” but it should say Rabbi Elazar, as in [Yevamot 96b](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.96b), where a Torah scroll was torn in their anger—and in [Mikvaot 6:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Mikvaot.6.1), [Niddah 1:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Niddah.1.5), and [Oholot 1:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Oholot.1.6). He disagreed with Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok in [Kelim 2:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kelim.2.6); Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in [Oholot 1:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Oholot.1.6); Rabbi Nehorai at the end of [Nazir](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Nazir.9); Rabbi Natan the Babylonian in [Shabbat 70a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.70a); Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in [Demai 6:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Demai.6.3), [Kelim 26:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kelim.26.1), and [Bava Metzia 8:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Metzia.8.8), where an incident was brought before both of them and they said to divide the intercalary month; and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri in [Kelim 8:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kelim.8.1).

Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Akiva’s son, was also his colleague: he called him simply “Yehoshua” in [Shevuot 6a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shevuot.6a). Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha likewise held him in great esteem, calling him Rabbi Yossi Beribbi in *Sifra*, Shemini, chapter 9. As for [Yoma 8a](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.8a), where he appears in a dispute with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Chanina, deputy high priest: this undoubtedly reflects the work of the arrangers of the baraitot, since Rabbi Chanina’s opinion mediates between Rabbi Meir’s and Rabbi Yossi’s.[^3]
**His well-known rulings in the Mishnah and Gemara.**

One who recites the Shema without making it audible to his own ears has not fulfilled his obligation; one who fails to articulate its letters precisely has fulfilled it—[Berakhot 2:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Berakhot.2.3).
Anyone who departs from the formula established by the sages for blessings has not fulfilled his obligation—[Berakhot 40b](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.40b).

Mother onions are exempt from pe’ah—[Pe’ah 3:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Peah.3.4). The law of forgotten produce does not apply to olive trees—[Pe’ah, beginning of chapter 7](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Peah.7.1).[^9]

A person cannot consecrate what does not belong to him—[Kilayim 7:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kilayim.7.5). The *adnei ha-sadeh* convey impurity under a roof as a human does—[Kilayim 8:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kilayim.8.5). The wild ox belongs to the category of wild animals—[8:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kilayim.8.6). *Semadar* is forbidden as orlah because it is fruit—[Orlah 1:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Orlah.1.7).[^9]

An androgynos is a creature of a category of its own—[Bikkurim 4:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bikkurim.4.5). A *koy* likewise belongs to a category of its own—[Chullin 80a](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.80a).[^9]

If one extinguishes a lamp out of concern for it, Rabbi Yossi exempts him in all cases except concern for the wick—[Shabbat 2:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Shabbat.2.5), since he holds that work not needed for its own defining purpose does not incur liability. The Sabbath prohibition of kindling was singled out to establish a separate negative commandment—[Shabbat 70a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.70a).[^10]

An eruv whose validity is doubtful is valid—[Eruvin 3:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Eruvin.3.5). The high priest’s frontplate does not secure acceptance for the portions of offerings meant to be eaten—[Pesachim 77a](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.77a). If someone carries his lulav into the public domain on the Sabbath, he is exempt—[Sukkah 3:14](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Sukkah.3.14), because one who errs in carrying out a commandment and does perform a commandment is exempt. Women may voluntarily lay their hands on an offering—[Chagigah 16b](https://www.sefaria.org/Chagigah.16b).[^11]

A fetus disqualifies from eating terumah but does not confer the right to eat it—[Yevamot 7:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Yevamot.7.3). A priest who is an androgynos and marries an Israelite woman enables her to eat terumah—[Yevamot, end of chapter 8](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Yevamot.8.6). One who commits an offense carrying two possible death penalties is judged according to the first bond that made the relationship forbidden—[Yevamot 32a](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.32a).[^10]

Taking an object found by a deaf-mute, a person without legal capacity, or a minor is full-fledged theft—[Gittin 5:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Gittin.5.8), on the principle that one who has not acquired something may nevertheless be treated as having acquired it. “We told the messenger”—[Gittin, end of chapter 6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Gittin.6.7), since instructions alone cannot be delegated onward to another messenger. A man who has two sets of daughters may have all of them permitted to marry—[Kiddushin 3:9](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kiddushin.3.9), because a person does not place himself in a state of uncertainty.[^10]

If a male convert marries a female convert, their daughter is eligible to marry a priest—[Kiddushin 4:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kiddushin.4.6). A convert may marry a mamzeret—[Kiddushin 72b](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.72b).[^12]

“How can he do business with his neighbor’s cow?”—[Bava Metzia 3:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Metzia.3.2). “If so, what has the swindler lost?”—[3:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Metzia.3.4). They divide the intercalary month—[8:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Metzia.8.8).[^10]

When someone encloses his neighbor’s land, and the fourth side is then fenced, the whole cost is payable—[Bava Batra 1:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Batra.1.3). He permits mustard to remain beside bees—[2:10](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Batra.2.10), on the principle that it is the party causing damage who must distance himself. An *asmakhta* effects acquisition—[10:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Batra.10.5). One may write a receipt acknowledging repayment—[10:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Bava_Batra.10.6).[^10]

A witness whose testimony was discredited by alibi evidence in a monetary case remains eligible to testify in a capital case—[Sanhedrin 27b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.27b). Even on a weekday, consulting demons is forbidden—[Sanhedrin 101a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.101a). If both parties are disqualified from taking an oath, the oath returns to its original place—[Shevuot 7:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Shevuot.7.4).[^10]

A person going out to execution may make vows, undertake statutory valuation vows, and consecrate property—[Arakhin 1:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Arakhin.1.3). All seas can purify by their flowing water—[Parah 8:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Parah.8.8). With two paths, or two loaves one of which is impure, they are impure whichever way the matter is considered—[Tohorot 5:5–6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Tahorot.5.5-6).[^10]

He also customarily related incidents from earlier times, as in [Yoma 6:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Yoma.6.3), [Rosh Hashanah 1:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Rosh_Hashanah.1.7), [Eruvin 46b](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin.46b), [Chagigah 15b](https://www.sefaria.org/Chagigah.15b), and [Ketubot 105a](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.105a). He also transmitted testimony received from Shemaya and Avtalyon in [Yevamot 16a](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.16a). He interpreted dotted letters: in [Pesachim 9:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Pesachim.9.2), why the letter heh is dotted; and in [Menachot 87b](https://www.sefaria.org/Menachot.87b), why the vav is dotted.

There is no need to enumerate all his rulings: they fill the Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmuds, the Tosefta, Mekhilta, Sifra, Sifrei, and the midrashim. It appears clear that, in almost every midrashic passage where an unqualified Rabbi Yossi is mentioned, the person is not Rabbi Yossi ben Chalafta but Rabbi Yossi, the Palestinian amora who was Rabbi Yona’s colleague. Rabbi Huna spoke in his name several times. We shall give only some of his precious sayings in aggadah.[^13]

[Berakhot 7a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.7a): One should not try to appease someone while he is angry. A single chastening thought in a person’s heart is better than a hundred lashes. [Berakhot 53b](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.53b): One who answers “Amen” is greater than the person who recites the blessing. [Berakhot 60a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.60a): A person should not open his mouth to Satan. [Shabbat 12b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.12b): One who visits the sick should say, “May the Omnipresent have mercy on you among the sick of Israel.”

[Yoma 75a](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.75a): “See how the ways of the Holy One, blessed be He, differ from human ways. A human being who is angered by his fellow pursues him to the point of threatening his livelihood. The Holy One, blessed be He, does otherwise: He cursed the serpent, yet wherever it goes—even onto a roof—its food goes with it. He cursed woman, yet everyone runs after her. He cursed the earth, yet everyone is nourished from it.” And his remarkable saying in [Sukkah 5a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sukkah.5a): “The Divine Presence never descended below, and Moses and Elijah never ascended on high.”

[Chagigah 12b](https://www.sefaria.org/Chagigah.12b): “Woe to people who see but do not know what they see, who stand but do not know upon what they stand. On what does the earth stand? It hangs upon the arm of the Holy One, blessed be He.”

[Megillah 24b](https://www.sefaria.org/Megillah.24b): Rabbi Yossi said, “All my life I was troubled by the verse, ‘You shall grope at noon as the blind person gropes in darkness.’ What difference does darkness or light make to a blind person? Until once an incident came my way. I was walking in the dead of night, in darkness, and saw a blind man carrying a torch. I asked him, ‘My son, why do you need this torch?’ He answered: ‘As long as the torch is in my hand, people see me and save me from pits …’”

His precious saying in [Ta’anit 21b](https://www.sefaria.org/Taanit.21b): “It is not a person’s place that honors him; the person honors his place.” [Bava Metzia 71a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Metzia.71a): “See the blindness of those who lend at interest …” [Avot 4:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Pirkei_Avot.4.6): “Anyone who honors Torah is himself honored by people.”

He taught well and lived by what he taught. He made Torah a splendid crown, and without him we would grope like a blind person in darkness. His contribution was the precious baraita called *Seder Olam*. [Yevamot 82b](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.82b) and [Niddah 46b](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.46b) explicitly record Rabbi Yochanan’s statement: “Who is the tanna of Seder Olam? Rabbi Yossi.” The great scholar Rabbi Ber Ratner, may his light shine, has already treated this at length, with excellent judgment.

He was distinguished by what people always said of him: “Rabbi Yossi’s reasoning accompanies him”—[Eruvin 51a](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin.51a), [Gittin 67a](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.67a), and [Bekhorot 37a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.37a). Rashi explains: his explanation accompanies his rulings, supplying a reason for everything he says. Indeed, we find this in [Terumot 10:3 and 10:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Terumot.10), [Sukkah 3:14](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Sukkah.3.14), and [Yevamot 4:10](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Yevamot.4.10). In [Parah 3:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Parah.3.3), he says: “Do not give the Sadducees an opportunity to dominate.” In [Sifrei Devarim 13](https://www.sefaria.org/Sifrei_Devarim.13), Arios asks him, “Who is wise?” He answers: “One who puts his learning into practice.” He truly did put his learning into practice.[^20]
**His admirable character.**

He testified about himself in [Shabbat 118b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.118b): “I have never said something and looked behind me.” He never spoke slander about anyone; consequently, whenever he spoke, he feared no one and had no need to look behind him lest the person concerned hear him. “I have never looked at my circumcised organ. I have never disregarded my colleagues’ words. I know that I am not a priest, but if my colleagues tell me to ascend the platform, I ascend. The beams of my house have never seen the seams of my shirt.”[^14]

He also says there: “May my portion be with those who eat three meals on the Sabbath; those who complete Hallel each day; those who die of intestinal illness; those who die on the way to fulfill a commandment; those who bring in the Sabbath in Tiberias and see it out in Sepphoris; those who sit in the study house, not those who make people leave it; those who collect charity, not those who distribute it. May my portion be with those who are suspected but are innocent.”[^14]

The statement attributed to Rabbi Yossi there, “May my portion be with those who pray at twilight,” is better read as in [Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 4:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Berakhot.4.1), where Rabbi Yossi son of Rabbi Chanina says it. This also makes better sense of Rabba bar bar Chana’s statement in Rabbi Yochanan’s name that it is meritorious to pray at twilight. Conversely, [Gittin 56a](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.56a), “Rabbi Yochanan said: The humility of Rabbi Zechariah ben Avkulas …,” should read “Rabbi Yossi said,” because its source is [Tosefta Shabbat, chapter 16](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Shabbat.16), which correctly attributes it to Rabbi Yossi. It is also so in Lamentations Rabbah, the section “The children of Zion.” Rabbi Yochanan is not mentioned in the Tosefta.[^3]

He also says in [Shabbat 118a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.118a): “Anyone who delights in the Sabbath is granted an inheritance without boundaries.” His practice was to remain silent, as befits a sage: [Shabbat 33b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.33b) says that Rabbi Yossi was silent. In [Nazir](https://www.sefaria.org/Nazir.52b), after Rabbi Meir’s death, Rabbi Yehuda said that Rabbi Meir’s pupils should not enter. Symmachus pressed his way in, and Rabbi Yehuda became angry. Rabbi Yossi said: “People will say: ‘Meir has died; Yehuda became angry; Yossi remained silent’—what will become of Torah?”

Perhaps he adopted this trait because of the incident related in [Yevamot 96b](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.96b): at the synagogue in Tiberias, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yossi disputed until a Torah scroll was torn in their anger. Rabbi Yossi ben Kisma was there and said, “I shall be surprised if this synagogue does not become a house of idolatry.” So it happened.[^3]

He valued his colleagues more than himself. [Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 2:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Berakhot.2.7) and [Moed Katan 3:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Moed_Katan.3.5), relate that, when Rabbi Meir came to his city, Rabbi Yossi told them: “He is a great man, a holy man, a modest man.” He was repaid measure for measure. [Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 3:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Berakhot.3.4), relates that people saw him immersing privately on Yom Kippur and said: “Can you say that such a holy person had forgotten?”[^15]

[Yoma 83b](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.83b) relates that Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yossi once traveled together. Rabbi Meir paid close attention to names; Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi did not. They came to an inn whose keeper was named Kidor. Rabbi Meir thought, “This shows that he is wicked,” and did not entrust his money to him. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi did. The innkeeper later denied having their money, and they recovered it only by a stratagem. From then on, they too paid attention to names. When they came to an innkeeper named Bala, they would not enter his establishment.

The same passage relates that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi were traveling when Rabbi Yehuda suffered a ravenous hunger attack. He compelled a shepherd and forcibly took his bread. Rabbi Yossi said: “You have deprived the shepherd!” When they reached a town, Rabbi Yossi suffered such an attack, and all its inhabitants brought him delicacies of every kind. Rabbi Yehuda then told him: “I deprived only the shepherd; you deprived the entire town.” [Nedarim 49b](https://www.sefaria.org/Nedarim.49b) also relates that, of Rabbi Yossi and Rabbi Yehuda, one ate porridge with his fingers and the other with a piece of palm leaf.

At the end of [Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 3:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Berakhot.3.4), it is related that Rabbi Yossi once traveled at night with a donkey-driver following him. They came to a pit, and the donkey-driver wished to immerse. Rabbi Yossi told him not to endanger himself. He replied that he had had intercourse with a menstruating woman and could not do otherwise. Rabbi Yossi said: “He will go down and will not come up.” So it happened.[^15]

We find in the midrash that a certain matron, a worshipper of the serpent, regularly debated with him, and he answered her wisely. [Genesis Rabbah 4](https://www.sefaria.org/Bereshit_Rabbah.4) relates that she asked why “it was good” is not written on the second day of creation. He answered: “Because the work involving water had not been completed; therefore ‘it was good’ is written twice on the third day.” In [chapter 17](https://www.sefaria.org/Bereshit_Rabbah.17), she asked why God needed to take Adam’s rib by stealth. He replied with a comparison: “Someone secretly deposited silver with you, and you publicly returned gold to him—is that theft?”

At the beginning of [Genesis Rabbah 25](https://www.sefaria.org/Bereshit_Rabbah.25), she asked why no death is recorded for Enoch, although he was not completely righteous. He answered: “It is written, ‘He was no more, for God took him’”. In [chapter 23](https://www.sefaria.org/Bereshit_Rabbah.23), she asked why Esau emerged first. He answered that Jacob’s drop was first.[^16]

In [Genesis Rabbah 68:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Bereshit_Rabbah.68.4), she asked what God had been doing since creating the world. He answered: “He sits and makes matches.” She said: “I too can do that in a short time.” He replied: “It may seem easy to you, but for Him it is as difficult as splitting the Red Sea.” She took a thousand male slaves and a thousand female slaves and paired them. The next morning they came to her with injured heads, blinded eyes, and broken legs. She then summoned Rabbi Yossi ben Chalafta and said: “Your God is true, and your Torah is beautiful and praiseworthy.”[^13]

In [Genesis Rabbah 87](https://www.sefaria.org/Bereshit_Rabbah.87), she asked: “Could Joseph, a boy of seventeen, in all his youthful ardor, really have refrained from doing this?” He immediately read to her the accounts of Reuben and Bilhah and of Judah and Tamar. He said: “If Joseph had sinned, Scripture would not have concealed his sin, just as it did not conceal theirs.”

[Exodus Rabbah 3:12](https://www.sefaria.org/Shemot_Rabbah.3.12): She told him, “My god”—the serpent—“is greater than your God. When God appeared to Moses in the bush, Moses merely hid his face; when he saw the serpent, it says, ‘Moses fled.’” He answered: “When God appeared, where could Moses flee? God’s glory fills the whole world. But if he flees three steps from the serpent, he is immediately safe.”

[Numbers Rabbah 3:12](https://www.sefaria.org/Bamidbar_Rabbah.3.12): She told him, “Your God bestows good even though He is not just”—meaning that He does not distinguish between people. He brought before her a basket of figs, and she selected the good ones and ate them. He said: “You know how to choose the good ones, and God does not?”

[Ecclesiastes Rabbah 1:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Kohelet_Rabbah.1.7): They asked him about “He gives wisdom to the wise.” Should it not say, “He gives wisdom to fools”? He replied: “If two people came to borrow money from you, one rich and the other poor, to which would you lend?” She answered: “To the rich one.” He said: “Let your ears hear what your mouth is saying.” At the end of [chapter 3](https://www.sefaria.org/Kohelet_Rabbah.3), they asked about “Who knows whether the spirit of human beings rises upward?” He answered: “These are the souls of the righteous …”

In [Tanchuma, Bereishit](https://www.sefaria.org/Midrash_Tanchuma%2C_Bereshit), the argument is made from “That your days may be multiplied … as the days of heaven upon the earth”: you endure only as long as heaven and earth endure, and heaven and earth will eventually wear out. He answered: “From the very place you brought evidence, I shall bring evidence for the opposite …” In *Pesikta Rabbati*, the second chapter on the Ten Commandments, they asked why the letter lamed rises higher than all other letters. He answered: “Because it is a herald”—it proclaims “Learn!”—“and a herald customarily stands in a high place to proclaim.”
**His pupils and those who transmitted his teachings.**

Although we do not find many pupils identified by name, he undoubtedly had many. Besides his sons, who received teachings from him and whom we shall discuss below, we know that Rabbi Judah the Patriarch learned from him. In [Niddah 68b](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.68b), Rabbi says, “I asked Rabbi Yossi”; in [Menachot 14a](https://www.sefaria.org/Menachot.14a), he speaks in Rabbi Yossi’s name. Rabbi held him in such esteem that, when Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yossi conveyed a ruling to him in his father’s name, he would say: “The elder has already ruled.” His words were like those of the Urim, admitting no questioning—[Shabbat 51a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.51a) and [Yevamot 105b](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.105b). When Rabbi wished to challenge Rabbi Yossi’s words, he said in [Jerusalem Talmud, Gittin 6:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Gittin.6.7), “We, the lowly ones … As the Holy of Holies differs from the ordinary, so our generation differs from Rabbi Yossi’s generation.”[^17]

Issi ben Yehuda was also his pupil. [Nedarim 81a](https://www.sefaria.org/Nedarim.81a) relates that Issi ben Yehuda did not come to Rabbi Yossi’s academy for three days. Vardimos, Rabbi Yossi’s son, found him and asked why he was not coming to the study house. He answered: “I do not understand your father’s reasoning …” In [Jerusalem Talmud, Shevi’it 8:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sheviit.8.5), Yehuda of Hutza questions Rabbi Yossi ben Chalafta, who tells his son Avradimos to answer him.

Yehuda ben Agra speaks in his name in [Niddah 52b–53a](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.52b-53a). Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda speaks in his name in [Ma’aser Sheni 3:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Maaser_Sheni.3.6) and [Makkot 20a](https://www.sefaria.org/Makkot.20a). Rabbi Shimon ben Yossi ben Lekonya questions him in [Zevachim 62b](https://www.sefaria.org/Zevachim.62b). Rabbi Yossi said of Symmachus: “These are nothing but words of prophecy”—[Bava Batra 12a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.12a). *Seder ha-Dorot* cites Rabbi Elazar of the South as questioning Rabbi Yossi. With respect, its author erred: he did not recognize that Rabbi Elazar of the South was one of the later amoraim and was a pupil of Rabbi Yossi, Rabbi Yona’s colleague.
**His wife and children.**

Although his wife’s name is not recorded, the beginning of [Jerusalem Talmud, Yevamot](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Yevamot.1.1), explicitly says that she had been the wife of his brother, who died, and that Rabbi Yossi married her through levirate marriage. They lived happily together. As he says in [Shabbat 118b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.118b), “I never called my wife ‘my wife,’ but ‘my home.’” [Genesis Rabbah 68:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Bereshit_Rabbah.68.3), relates that she once quarreled with her female servant, and Rabbi Yossi upheld the servant’s case in his wife’s presence. His wife said: “Why do you contradict me before my servant?” He answered: “Did Job not say, ‘If I rejected the claim of my male or female servant’?”

She bore him five fine sons. In [Shabbat 118b](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.118b), he says, “I planted five cedars in Israel”: Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Chalafta, Rabbi Avtilas, and Rabbi Menachem. Rabbi Menachem is also called Vardimos, because his face resembled a rose; in the Jerusalem Talmud passage cited above, he is called Avradimos. [Genesis Rabbah 84:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Bereshit_Rabbah.84.5), says that his eyes were *zamran*, like vine shoots, and resembled his mother’s.[^18]

The eldest was Rabbi Yishmael, who was Rabbi Judah the Patriarch’s colleague and received many teachings from his father. His father also transmitted valuable information concerning Jewish history to him, as explained in his entry. Rabbi Elazar, another son, was also a leading sage of the generation. In [Pesachim 107a](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.107a), Rabbi Yossi says: “My son Eliezer says … His colleagues disagree with him, but his words seem better than theirs.” [Me’ilah 17b](https://www.sefaria.org/Meilah.17b), relates that, when a delegation once had to go to Rome to annul decrees, they sent Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai and Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yossi. Rabbi Yossi feared to send his son with Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, lest the latter become angry and punish him, until Rabbi Shimon undertook not to punish him.

Vardimos, his son, was also a Torah scholar, as [Nedarim 81a](https://www.sefaria.org/Nedarim.81a) and [Shevi’it 8:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sheviit.8.8) indicate. Rabbi Chalafta, his son, was the father of the well-known Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta, as I explained in that sage’s entry. We also find a report that a son died during Rabbi Yossi’s lifetime: [Moed Katan 21a](https://www.sefaria.org/Moed_Katan.21a) relates that, when Rabbi Yossi’s son died in Sepphoris, he entered the study house and lectured all day. *Yuchasin* identifies that son as Rabbi Chalafta, without any evidence. It seems more likely that no son of Rabbi Yossi died during his lifetime: the passage in Moed Katan should read “the son of Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili,” as it appears in [Semachot, chapter 10](https://www.sefaria.org/Tractate_Semachot.10).[^3]
**His death.**

Apparently Rabbi Yossi died before Rabbi Yehuda. This is suggested by [Sukkah 18a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sukkah.18a): when Rabbi Yehuda lectured, Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yossi told him, “My master! This is how Father explained it … This is what Father said.” *Kaftor va-Ferach*, chapter 6, page 107, in the Luncz edition, quotes [Jerusalem Talmud, Moed Katan 3:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Moed_Katan.3.7): “When Rabbi Yehuda died, Rabbi Yossi ruled that the torn garment could be loosely stitched the next day.” This is a textual error and should read: “When Rabbi Yochanan died, Rabbi Yasa ruled”—Rabbi Yasa being Rabbi Assi. This is clear.[^19]

He died in his birthplace, Sepphoris. [Moed Katan 25b](https://www.sefaria.org/Moed_Katan.25b) says that, when Rabbi Yossi died, the gutters of Sepphoris flowed with blood. [Jerusalem Talmud, Avodah Zarah 3:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Avodah_Zarah.3.1), says that, when Rabbi Yossi ben Chalafta died, the pipes ran with blood in Laodicea. They said that he gave his life for the converts.[^22] As is known, all the sages of that generation were called “our masters in the south,” meaning Lod. *Erekh Millin*, page 155, and *Sheva Chokhmot*, under “Sepphoris,” say that [Bava Metzia 84b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Metzia.84b) should read “Your father fled to Laodicea; you fled to Asia,” reversing our version. We have no need of that change.[^3]

At the end of [Jerusalem Talmud, Sotah](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sotah.9), they eulogized him in a few words: “When Rabbi Yossi died, understanding ceased.” Thus his son Rabbi Yishmael says in [Jerusalem Talmud, Gittin 6:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Gittin.6.7): “As gold differs from dust, so our generation differs from the generation of my father Rabbi Yossi.” Of him we may say the precious words at the end of [Kelim](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Kelim.30.4): “Fortunate are you, Rabbi Yossi, who entered in impurity and came out in purity.”

notes.text: Hyman’s opening identifies the usual unqualified tannaitic “Rabbi Yossi” with Rabbi Yossi ben Chalafta. It is not a rule equating every occurrence across all periods: this article itself distinguishes the Palestinian amora Rabbi Yossi, Rabbi Yossi ha-Kohen, Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili, Rabbi Yossi ben Chanina, and Rabbi Yasa/Assi.

Hyman compares variant speaker attributions in Yoma and Menachot, Rashi, and *Dikdukei Soferim*. The disagreement is part of his argument and has been retained. The “ramp” belongs to the Yom Kippur scapegoat procedure; the other passage concerns sacrificial food. The parenthetic account of hostility to Babylonians reflects the cited source’s language.

Chronology, ancestry arguments, assessments of earlier scholars, and proposed emendations are Hyman’s views. His confident language is translated faithfully without converting it into independently established history. His proposals about Rabbi Elazar/Eliezer, the twilight prayer, Rabbi Zechariah ben Avkulas, and the deceased son remain proposals attributed to him. Bibliographical abbreviations are expanded where their identification is established; דה״ד is retained because its exact bibliographical expansion has not been independently established here. Uncertain printed references are not silently repaired.

“Asia” renders אסיא, the ancient destination named in these sources; it should not be assumed to mean the entire modern continent. Hyman’s reconstruction of destruction, flight, confinement, and resettlement is presented as his argument. The figure of 130,000 marketplaces belongs to the quoted rabbinic account.

Hyman prints ברכות ס., “Berakhot 60a,” for the calendar controversy involving Chananya. The linked passage is **Berakhot 63a**, where that controversy appears; the original reference is retained here. The Hebrew transcription retains the printed reference.

ערכי means the city’s judicial records/court context, not a valuation procedure here. בא״ז is expanded as “in the privy.” The ordinance sought to make a woman’s presence audible and protect her from assault; Hyman’s parenthetic explanation of resettlement and the abduction is retained as his explanation.

Hyman prints יבמות סג:, “Yevamot 63b,” for Rabbi Yossi’s question to Elijah about the helpmate. The linked discussion is **Yevamot 63a**. Folio corrections here affect only the English reference link and this note.

Hyman’s Bikkurim exception concerns the first three chapters, as he explicitly explains; the fourth chapter is transmitted separately in some editions. His six order totals sum to 340. The printed Avot numbering is retained: editions differ in the division of individual mishnayot, so the linked location may use a different subdivision. The historical namesake distinction is Hyman’s, not an automatic identity merge.

Pe’ah is the share of field produce left for the poor; shikhchah is produce inadvertently left behind; orlah is the prohibition on fruit during a tree’s first three years. “Mother onions” translates אמהות של בצלים. *Adnei ha-sadeh* is the creature discussed under that rabbinic name, not a modern zoological identification. *Semadar* is the blossom/early formation of a grape cluster. An androgynos has both male and female sexual characteristics; a *koy* is an animal whose classification as domestic or wild is uncertain. These are technical legal categories in the cited texts.

Hyman gives brief headings for complex legal discussions. They are translated as summaries, not practical rulings. An *asmakhta* is a conditional undertaking made without an unqualified intention to incur the stated obligation. “The oath returns to its original place” is the cited formulation, whose consequences are debated. The two paths and two loaves concern uncertainty about ritual impurity. In the rented-cow and intercalary-month cases, the fuller facts are supplied by the linked mishnayot.

Hyman prints סוכה פ״ג מ״ד, “Sukkah 3:4,” for carrying the lulav on the Sabbath and repeats that reference later. In the linked Mishnah division, the passage is **Sukkah 3:14**. His printed reference is retained in this note. “Frontplate” renders the high priest’s tzitz; laying hands on an offering renders semikhah, not rabbinic ordination.

*Mamzeret* is the female form of the technical lineage category mamzer, concerning birth from certain forbidden unions; it does not mean simply a child born outside marriage. Hyman’s terse “a convert marries a mamzeret” is rendered as the permissive ruling in context.

Hyman warns that many midrashic “Rabbi Yossi” passages belong to the later Palestinian amora. His ensuing selection nevertheless includes narratives associated with Rabbi Yossi ben Chalafta. In the matchmaking story the print abbreviates the speaker as ריב״ח; the corresponding **Genesis Rabbah 68:4** names Rabbi Yossi ben Chalafta in full, supporting the expansion used here. The English links do not silently settle every other namesake attribution.

The autobiographical statements “I have never …,” the five sons, and “my wife, my home” occur on **Shabbat 118b** in the linked edition; Hyman sometimes prints קיח., “118a,” for them. His instruction about Hallel is a compressed quotation: the Talmud distinguishes the prohibited daily recitation of the complete festival Hallel from the psalms intended here. “The seams of my shirt” is a statement of personal modesty, not a claim about ordinary visibility of clothing.

The Jerusalem Talmud’s compact wording about immersion on Yom Kippur and the donkey-driver is difficult and edition-dependent. The first remark questions whether a person so holy could have forgotten to immerse; the linked Jerusalem Talmud discusses forgetting an immersion before Yom Kippur. בעל נדה in the second story is rendered as someone who had intercourse with a menstruating woman; the obligation and dangers of immersion belong to the ancient account.

Hyman’s parenthetic ש״ס שבת in the Enoch discussion is compressed/unclear; the English gives the contrast in the quoted reply rather than inventing a new source attribution. The corresponding Genesis Rabbah passage understands “God took him” as Enoch’s death; that explanation belongs to the source comparison, rather than added words in Hyman’s quoted reply. “Jacob’s drop was first” refers to the story’s explanation of conception and birth order, not a modern embryological assertion.

“Rabbi,” without a personal name, means Rabbi Judah the Patriarch in this section. The Urim are the sacred means of consultation associated with the high priest; Hyman’s comparison expresses the authority Rabbi accorded Rabbi Yossi’s rulings. Recounting a teaching in another sage’s name does not by itself establish direct teacher–student contact.

Hyman identifies Menachem with Vardimos/Avradimos and describes the five sons and a grandson. These identifications are retained as his statements. *Zamran* is preserved with Hyman’s own vine-shoot explanation; the description of the eyes is not turned into a medical diagnosis.

Hyman quotes the Luncz edition’s Rabbi Yehuda/Rabbi Yossi wording and explicitly proposes Rabbi Yochanan/Rabbi Yasa instead. Both are kept here as quotation and proposed correction; the English does not treat the corrected reading as the unchanged printed witness. Loose stitching refers to a garment torn in mourning.

Hyman prints “Sifrei Devarim—53” and the name אריס. The matching passage is **Sifrei Devarim 13**, whose named questioner is אריוס, rendered “Arios” here. The speaker’s further historical identification is not settled by this name. The printed name and reference remain recorded in this note.

Hyman’s transcription reads מודה אבא חלפתא בזה שהוא טועה, “Father Chalafta admits that he is mistaken in this.” The linked **Bekhorot 26a** reads שהוא מותר, “that this is permitted.” The English uses that source reading and records Hyman’s divergent wording here; the Hebrew article is unchanged.

Hyman quotes דהיב נפשיה על גוירתא immediately after reporting Rabbi Yossi ben Chalafta’s death. “Gave his life” is a literal rendering: the expression can convey devotion or the sacrifice of his life. The passage does not explicitly describe the circumstances or cause of his death.

Hyman cites Song of Songs Rabbah פ״ב־ג, “2–3.” The gathering at Usha appears in **2:5** in the linked division. That witness spells the son of Rabbi Yossi ha-Gelili’s name אליעזר, rendered “Eliezer” here; Hyman abbreviates it ר״א.
